concept.name: Rolling Deployment Strategy

relationships.description: Connects Rolling Deployment Strategy to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: A rolling deployment incrementally replaces old service instances with new ones in bounded batches (e.g., maxSurge 25%, maxUnavailable 0) gated by readiness probes and connection draining, achieving zero downtime without doubling infrastructure capacity.
spark.keyTakeaway: Zero-downtime rolling updates require three synchronized invariants: backward-compatible schemas/APIs during the overlap window, accurate readiness probes before shifting traffic, and pre-stop connection draining after SIGTERM.

concept.whyItMatters: Deploying a new binary simultaneously across all instances causes immediate downtime, while full blue-green environments double peak compute bills for large clusters. Rolling deployments let teams ship dozens of times per day on existing capacity (10-25% surge) while isolating bad builds before they reach 100% of users.
whenToUse: Stateless microservices and web APIs running on orchestrators (Kubernetes, AWS ECS, Nomad) where v1 and v2 can coexist safely.
Cost-sensitive clusters where maintaining a 100% duplicate idle green fleet is prohibitively expensive.
Routine continuous delivery pipelines (10-50 deploys/day) paired with automated readiness gates and metric-based rollbacks.
whenNotToUse: Monolithic databases or stateful single-leader systems requiring an exclusive schema lock or incompatible wire-protocol switch.
High-risk releases needing instant 100%-to-0% traffic cutover or isolated dark-launch validation (prefer Blue-Green or Canary).
Legacy stateful apps that hold unshared in-memory sessions without sticky routing or externalized Redis session stores.
keyPoints: maxSurge controls extra capacity spun up during rollout (e.g., 25%), while maxUnavailable=0 guarantees full serving capacity at every step.
Readiness probes (/readyz) gate when a new pod enters the load-balancer EndpointSlice; liveness probes (/livez) only restart wedged processes.
Asynchronous EndpointSlice/kube-proxy propagation takes 1-5s; a preStop sleep (5-15s) prevents in-flight 502s after SIGTERM.
Because v1 and v2 run concurrently for minutes, every DB migration and internal message schema must follow the expand-and-contract pattern.
PodDisruptionBudgets (PDB) protect minimum replica counts when node drains or cluster upgrades overlap with a rolling deploy.

examples.title: Eliminating 502 Spikes During Kubernetes Deploys
examples.scenario: A 40-pod Go payment API saw 150-300 HTTP 502 errors on every deploy because pods exited immediately on SIGTERM while kube-proxy iptables rules still routed traffic for ~3 seconds.
examples.outcome: Adding a 10s preStop lifecycle sleep, setting terminationGracePeriodSeconds=45, and sending HTTP/2 GOAWAY before draining dropped deploy-time 502s to zero.

examples.title: Zero-Downtime Column Rename via Expand-Contract
examples.scenario: Renaming user_name to handle in a 500M-row PostgreSQL table broke v1 pods the instant v2's migration ran during a rolling update.
examples.outcome: Splitting the change into 3 deploys—(1) add handle + dual-write trigger, (2) backfill + deploy v2 reading handle, (3) drop user_name—enabled a zero-downtime rolling rollout.

tradeOffs.pro: Larger batches (e.g., 50% surge) finish rollouts in 2 steps, shrinking the risky v1+v2 overlap window.
tradeOffs.con: Increases transient CPU/RAM cost and widens the blast radius if a bad build passes /readyz.

tradeOffs.pro: Rolling updates require only 10-25% headroom instead of 100% duplicate fleet capacity.
tradeOffs.con: Rollbacks are slower (must roll forward/reverse batch by batch) and v1/v2 must be mutually compatible.

tradeOffs.factor: Strict Readiness Gates vs Fast Startup
tradeOffs.pro: Checking downstream dependencies or warm caches in /readyz prevents cold-start latency spikes.
tradeOffs.con: If /readyz checks external DBs, a brief DB blip can mark all pods unready and cause a full-cluster outage.

failureModes.name: SIGTERM vs Load-Balancer Propagation Race
failureModes.description: The orchestrator sends SIGTERM and terminates the process before iptables/IPVS/ALB targets finish removing the pod IP, causing connection resets.
failureModes.mitigation: Fail /readyz immediately on SIGTERM, execute a preStop hook (sleep 10s) to let LB endpoints drain, and only then stop the HTTP listener.

failureModes.name: Breaking Schema or Serialization Skew
failureModes.description: v2 pods write a new protobuf field or drop a SQL column that still-running v1 pods expect, crashing v1 workers mid-rollout.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce N-1 backward compatibility in CI (protobuf field deprecation, expand-contract DB migrations) before any rolling deploy.

failureModes.name: Readiness Probe Cascading Failure
failureModes.description: Putting a hard dependency check (e.g., SELECT 1 on Postgres) inside /readyz causes every pod to drop out of the LB simultaneously during a 2s DB hiccup.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep /readyz focused on local process readiness (listener bound, caches warmed) and handle transient upstream errors with circuit breakers.

failureModes.name: Slow Rollout Stalling on Resource Quotas
failureModes.description: With maxSurge=25% and tight namespace CPU limits or node capacity, new v2 pods stay Pending forever while v1 pods cannot scale down when maxUnavailable=0.
failureModes.mitigation: Maintain 15-25% cluster headroom for autoscaling/surges, set minReadySeconds appropriately, and configure progressDeadlineSeconds to alert on stalled rollouts.

commonMistakes: Using the same endpoint for livenessProbe and readinessProbe, causing Kubernetes to kill-loop pods that are merely overloaded.
Leaving terminationGracePeriodSeconds at 30s for workers that run 90s batch jobs or long-lived WebSockets.
Setting maxUnavailable > 0 on small 2-replica services, silently dropping capacity by 50% during peak traffic.
Omitting minReadySeconds (default 0), which lets a rollout declare success the instant a pod passes one probe even if it crashes 5s later.
Forgetting to configure connection draining on external cloud load balancers (ALB deregistration_delay).

sections.content:
## The idea

A rolling deployment updates a fleet of $N$ identical instances by replacing a bounded subset at a time—creating a surge of new `v2` instances, waiting until they pass readiness checks, draining connections from `v1` instances, and terminating `v1` only after in-flight requests finish.

Unlike a Blue-Green cutover (which requires $2N$ capacity) or a Recreate deploy (which incurs downtime), a rolling update runs on $N + \text{maxSurge}$ capacity—typically 10% to 25% extra headroom—while maintaining 100% serving availability when `maxUnavailable: 0`.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a 10-pod Kubernetes `Deployment` configured with `maxSurge: 2`, `maxUnavailable: 0`, `minReadySeconds: 15`, and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45`:

1. **Surge v2 Pods**: The Deployment controller scales the `v2` ReplicaSet to 2 pods (`10 v1 + 2 v2` total). `v2` pods load config and bind port `8080`.
2. **Readiness Gate**: `kubelet` polls `GET /readyz` every `5s`. Once `v2` returns `200 OK` twice, the EndpointSlice controller adds the `v2` pod IPs to the Service.
3. **Wait `minReadySeconds`**: The controller waits `15s` to verify `v2` does not crash-loop under live traffic before marking those 2 pods available.
4. **Drain v1 Pods**: The controller marks 2 `v1` pods for termination: EndpointSlice removes their IPs while `kubelet` runs `preStop: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]` so `kube-proxy`/Envoy finishes syncing.
5. **Graceful Shutdown**: After `10s`, `v1` receives `SIGTERM`, sends HTTP/2 `GOAWAY`, finishes active requests within `35s`, and exits cleanly. The loop repeats in batches of 2 until all 10 pods are `v2`.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Managing the v1 + v2 overlap window
sections.content:
## Managing the v1 + v2 overlap window

During a rolling deploy, `v1` and `v2` run side by side for 2 to 15 minutes. Any shared state—databases, Redis keys, Kafka topics, or session cookies—must tolerate both versions concurrently:

- **Database Schemas**: Use expand-and-contract. Add nullable columns or new tables first, deploy code that dual-writes, backfill historical rows, switch reads to the new column, and drop the old column in a final deploy.
- **Wire & Cache Formats**: Never reuse protobuf field numbers or mutate JSON field types in place. Version Redis cache keys (e.g., `user:v2:{id}`) when payload structure changes.

## Deployment strategies compared

| Strategy | Peak Capacity | Downtime | Rollback Speed | Blast Radius Control |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Rolling Update** | 110%-125% (`maxSurge`) | Zero (with `preStop`) | Minutes (batch reverse) | Batch-sized; pauses on failed readiness |
| **Blue-Green** | 200% (full duplicate) | Zero | Seconds (LB flip) | All-or-nothing at cutover |
| **Canary** | 105%-110% | Zero | Seconds (weight to 0%) | 1%-5% traffic slice gated by SLOs |
| **Recreate** | 100% | Full outage during boot | Minutes (re-pull old tag) | 100% (only for exclusive-lock workloads) |

## Failure modes

- **Graceful Shutdown Bypass**: Frameworks that do not trap `SIGTERM` (or apps wrapped in `sh -c` without `exec`) ignore the shutdown signal and get `SIGKILL`ed after `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, aborting active requests.
- **Silent Crash-Loop Rollout**: If `minReadySeconds` is `0` and the app crashes 10s after passing `/readyz` (e.g., on first real query), Kubernetes considers the surge pod "available" and proceeds to kill healthy `v1` pods.
- **PDB Deadlock**: Setting a `PodDisruptionBudget` with `minAvailable: 100%` blocks node drains, while `maxUnavailable: 0` without `maxSurge > 0` freezes the Deployment.

## Automated halt and rollback gates

Readiness probes only verify that a pod can accept TCP/HTTP traffic—they do not catch business-logic regressions (e.g., HTTP 500s on `/checkout` or 3x p99 latency).

- Pair rolling updates with a controller like **Argo Rollouts** or **Flagger** querying Prometheus every `30s` for 5xx rate (`<0.5%`) and p99 latency (`<250ms`).
- Configure `progressDeadlineSeconds: 600` so stuck rollouts surface immediately in CI/CD rather than hanging silently.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Set `maxUnavailable: 0` and `maxSurge: 25%` (or `1` for small replica sets) to preserve 100% capacity.
- [ ] Use `exec` in container entrypoints so `PID 1` receives `SIGTERM` directly.
- [ ] Add a `preStop` sleep (`5-15s`) and set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` > longest request timeout.
- [ ] Separate `/readyz` (local listener/cache ready) from `/livez` (deadlock check only).
- [ ] Set `minReadySeconds: 15-30` and `progressDeadlineSeconds: 600`.
- [ ] Enforce expand-and-contract migrations so `v1` and `v2` never clash on shared DBs or caches.

interviewProblems.title: Rolling Deployment Strategy
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Rolling Deployment Strategy. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A rolling deployment incrementally replaces old service instances with new ones in bounded batches (e.g., maxSurge 25%, maxUnavailable 0) gated by readiness probes and connection draining, achieving zero downtime without doubling infrastructure capacity.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: v2 ReplicaSet Pods applies the primary invariant and coordinates with v1 ReplicaSet Pods.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, v1 ReplicaSet Pods experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Fail /readyz immediately on SIGTERM, execute a preStop hook (sleep 10s) to let LB endpoints drain, and only then stop the HTTP listener.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Zero-downtime rolling updates require three synchronized invariants: backward-compatible schemas/APIs during the overlap window, accurate readiness probes before shifting traffic, and pre-stop connection draining after SIGTERM.
Avoid trap: Using the same endpoint for livenessProbe and readinessProbe, causing Kubernetes to kill-loop pods that are merely overloaded.
Avoid trap: Leaving terminationGracePeriodSeconds at 30s for workers that run 90s batch jobs or long-lived WebSockets.
When to reach for it: Stateless microservices and web APIs running on orchestrators (Kubernetes, AWS ECS, Nomad) where v1 and v2 can coexist safely.
When to reach for it: Cost-sensitive clusters where maintaining a 100% duplicate idle green fleet is prohibitively expensive.

putItTogether.title: Putting Rolling Deployment Strategy Together
putItTogether.summary: Zero-downtime rolling updates require three synchronized invariants: backward-compatible schemas/APIs during the overlap window, accurate readiness probes before shifting traffic, and pre-stop connection draining after SIGTERM.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Rolling Deployment Strategy before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Adding a 10s preStop lifecycle sleep, setting terminationGracePeriodSeconds=45, and sending HTTP/2 GOAWAY before draining dropped deploy-time 502s to zero.
